Task 1.a Discussion¶

The training dataset contains 428 articles and the testing dataset contains 106 articles. Using CountVectorizer, a total of 13,518 unique features were extracted from the training data.Each feature corresponds to a unique word appearing in the dataset. The resulting feature vectors represent the frequency of each word in each article using a bag-of-words representation. The dataset has already been preprocessed with tokenization, lower-casing, and removal of stop words and special characters, making it suitable for direct feature extraction.

Task 2: Classification Models Learning¶

Task 2.a: Naive Bayes Classification¶

I used the Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier because it is suitable for text classification with count-based features. The input features were produced by CountVectorizer, where each feature represents the frequency of one word in an article. The model estimates how likely each word is to appear in each class, such as P(word | tech) and P(word | entertainment). These probabilities can then be used to identify words that are strongly associated with each news category.

In [ ]:
nb_model = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)
nb_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

nb_pred = nb_model.predict(X_test)
nb_f1 = f1_score(y_test, nb_pred, average="weighted")

nb_report = classification_report(y_test, nb_pred, output_dict=True)
nb_report_df = pd.DataFrame(nb_report).transpose()

display(nb_report_df)
print(f"Weighted F1: {nb_f1:.4f}")

The precision and recall values for both classes are high. The top predictive words are the words with the highest conditional probability within each class.

For the entertainment class, words such as "film", "music", "actor", "awards", "band", and "star" are meaningful because they are strongly related to movies, music, and celebrity news.

For the tech class, words such as "mobile", "technology", "users", "software", "games", and "phone" are meaningful because they are commonly used in technology-related articles.

The discriminative word ratio was calculated as:

P(word | tech) / P(word | entertainment)

A large ratio means that the word is much more likely to appear in tech articles than in entertainment articles. For example, words such as "users", "software", "microsoft", "mobile", "broadband", and "virus" have very high ratios, so they are strong indicators of the tech class.

Similarly, words with very small ratios are more strongly associated with entertainment articles.

Overall, the discriminative ratio list describes the two classes better than the top predictive word list.

This is because the predictive word list mainly shows words with high frequency inside each class, while some common words such as "said" and "new" appear frequently in both classes.

In contrast, the discriminative ratio directly compares the probabilities between the two classes, making it more effective for identifying words that clearly separate tech and entertainment news.

2D training shape: (428, 2)

In [ ]:
def plot_knn_decision_boundary(X_2d, y, k=5, metric="euclidean"):
    label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
    y_encoded = label_encoder.fit_transform(y)
    # Train kNN on 2D PCA features
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, metric=metric)
    model.fit(X_2d, y_encoded)
    # Create a grid of points
    x_min, x_max = X_2d[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X_2d[:, 0].max() + 0.5
    y_min, y_max = X_2d[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X_2d[:, 1].max() + 0.5

    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(
        np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 300),
        np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 300)
    )

    grid_points = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]
    Z = model.predict(grid_points)
    Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3)

    scatter = plt.scatter(
        X_2d[:, 0],
        X_2d[:, 1],
        c=y_encoded,
        edgecolor="k",
        s=35
    )

    plt.xlabel("PCA Component 1")
    plt.ylabel("PCA Component 2")
    plt.title(f"kNN Decision Boundary, k={k}, metric={metric}")
    plt.legend(
        handles=scatter.legend_elements()[0],
        labels=list(label_encoder.classes_)
    )
    plt.show()
In [ ]:
# small k
plot_knn_decision_boundary(X_train_2d, y_train, k=3, metric="euclidean")

# larger k
plot_knn_decision_boundary(X_train_2d, y_train, k=15, metric="euclidean")

#different distance metric
plot_knn_decision_boundary(X_train_2d, y_train, k=5, metric="manhattan")

For the decision boundary plot, I used PCA to reduce the TF-IDF feature vectors into two dimensions. This makes it possible to visualize the kNN classifier in a 2D space.

When k is small, such as k = 3, the decision boundary is more flexible and irregular. This is because the prediction depends on only a few nearby points, so the model is more sensitive to local patterns and possible noise.

When k is larger, such as k = 15, the decision boundary becomes smoother. This is because the prediction uses more neighbours, so the model is less affected by individual points. However, if k is too large, the model may become too simple and may underfit the data.

The distance metric also changes the decision boundary because it changes how the nearest neighbours are selected. Euclidean distance and Manhattan distance measure distance in different ways, so they can produce different boundary shapes. Overall, k mainly controls the smoothness of the boundary, while the distance metric controls how similarity between articles is measured.

Task 2(c): Support Vector Machine (SVM)¶

In this section, we train two SVM classifiers:

  1. Soft-margin linear SVM
  2. Hard-margin RBF kernel SVM

We compare their decision boundaries and analyze the effect of hyperparameters such as C and gamma.

Linear SVM F1 Score: 0.9811799289034726

Linear SVM Analysis¶

A linear SVM was trained using TF-IDF features.
The hyperparameter C controls the penalty for misclassification.

  • Small C → smoother boundary, more regularization
  • Large C → stricter separation, possible overfitting

This model provides a baseline for comparison with the RBF kernel SVM.

In [ ]:
# RBF Kernel SVM
rbf_svm = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1000, gamma=0.01)

rbf_svm.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)

rbf_pred = rbf_svm.predict(X_test_tfidf)

rbf_f1 = f1_score(y_test, rbf_pred, average='weighted')

print("RBF SVM F1 Score:", rbf_f1)

RBF SVM F1 Score: 0.971797848780413

RBF SVM Analysis¶

An RBF kernel SVM was trained to capture non-linear decision boundaries.

The hyperparameter gamma controls the influence of each training point.

  • Small gamma → smoother decision boundary
  • Large gamma → more complex boundary and possible overfitting

The parameter C controls how strongly the model penalizes misclassification. A larger C attempts to classify training examples more strictly.

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_svm_decision_boundary(model, X_2d, y, title):
    x_min, x_max = X_2d[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X_2d[:, 0].max() + 0.5
    y_min, y_max = X_2d[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X_2d[:, 1].max() + 0.5

    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(
        np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 300),
        np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 300)
    )

    grid = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]
    Z = model.predict(grid)
    Z = np.array([0 if label == "entertainment" else 1 for label in Z])
    Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

    y_numeric = np.array([0 if label == "entertainment" else 1 for label in y])

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3)
    plt.scatter(X_2d[:, 0], X_2d[:, 1], c=y_numeric, edgecolors="k", s=25)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel("PCA Component 1")
    plt.ylabel("PCA Component 2")
    plt.show()

SVM Decision Boundary Discussion¶

The decision boundaries were plotted using two-dimensional PCA features.
The original TF-IDF feature space is high-dimensional, so PCA was used to project the data into two dimensions for visualization.

The linear SVM produces a straight decision boundary, which works well when the two classes are approximately separable in the reduced space.

The RBF kernel SVM can create a non-linear decision boundary. This allows it to capture more complex class patterns, but it may also overfit if gamma or C is too large.

Task 2.d: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)¶

For the ANN experiment, I used the existing TF-IDF representation and then reduced it to 100 dense components with TruncatedSVD followed by standard scaling. This keeps the ANN optimization stable while preserving the main information from the text features. The network has one hidden layer, ReLU activation in the hidden layer, a two-unit softmax output layer, initial weights drawn uniformly from ([0, 0.1]), learning rate 0.01, and 100 training epochs.

In [ ]:
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD

class SimpleANNClassifier(BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin):
    """A simple one-hidden-layer neural network for binary text classification."""
    def __init__(self, hidden_units=20, learning_rate=0.01, epochs=100, batch_size=32,
                 init_low=0.0, init_high=0.1, random_state=42):
        self.hidden_units = hidden_units
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate
        self.epochs = epochs
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.init_low = init_low
        self.init_high = init_high
        self.random_state = random_state

    def _softmax(self, scores):
        shifted = scores - np.max(scores, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        exp_scores = np.exp(shifted)
        return exp_scores / np.sum(exp_scores, axis=1, keepdims=True)

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X)
        rng = np.random.default_rng(self.random_state)

        self.label_encoder_ = LabelEncoder()
        y_encoded = self.label_encoder_.fit_transform(y)
        self.classes_ = self.label_encoder_.classes_

        n_samples, n_features = X.shape
        n_classes = len(self.classes_)
        Y = np.eye(n_classes)[y_encoded]

        # Required initialisation: weights are drawn uniformly from [0, 0.1].
        self.W1_ = rng.uniform(self.init_low, self.init_high, size=(n_features, self.hidden_units))
        self.b1_ = np.zeros((1, self.hidden_units))
        self.W2_ = rng.uniform(self.init_low, self.init_high, size=(self.hidden_units, n_classes))
        self.b2_ = np.zeros((1, n_classes))
        self.loss_history_ = []

        indices = np.arange(n_samples)
        batch_size = n_samples if self.batch_size is None else self.batch_size

        for _ in range(self.epochs):
            rng.shuffle(indices)

            for start in range(0, n_samples, batch_size):
                batch_idx = indices[start:start + batch_size]
                X_batch = X[batch_idx]
                Y_batch = Y[batch_idx]
                m = len(batch_idx)

                # Forward pass
                Z1 = X_batch @ self.W1_ + self.b1_
                A1 = np.maximum(0, Z1)  # ReLU hidden units
                scores = A1 @ self.W2_ + self.b2_
                probs = self._softmax(scores)

                # Backpropagation for cross-entropy with softmax
                d_scores = (probs - Y_batch) / m
                dW2 = A1.T @ d_scores
                db2 = np.sum(d_scores, axis=0, keepdims=True)

                dA1 = d_scores @ self.W2_.T
                dZ1 = dA1 * (Z1 > 0)
                dW1 = X_batch.T @ dZ1
                db1 = np.sum(dZ1, axis=0, keepdims=True)

                self.W2_ -= self.learning_rate * dW2
                self.b2_ -= self.learning_rate * db2
                self.W1_ -= self.learning_rate * dW1
                self.b1_ -= self.learning_rate * db1

            # Binary/categorical cross-entropy on the full training data
            full_hidden = np.maximum(0, X @ self.W1_ + self.b1_)
            full_probs = self._softmax(full_hidden @ self.W2_ + self.b2_)
            loss = -np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(full_probs + 1e-12), axis=1))
            self.loss_history_.append(loss)

        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X)
        hidden = np.maximum(0, X @ self.W1_ + self.b1_)
        return self._softmax(hidden @ self.W2_ + self.b2_)

    def predict(self, X):
        pred_encoded = np.argmax(self.predict_proba(X), axis=1)
        return self.label_encoder_.inverse_transform(pred_encoded)

ANN hidden-unit discussion¶

With only 2 hidden units, the network has limited capacity, so it can only learn a simple non-linear representation of the article features. Increasing the hidden layer to 5 and 20 units gives the model more parameters and usually lowers the training cross-entropy because it can represent more topic-specific patterns. Moving to 40 hidden units gives even higher capacity, but the improvement can become smaller and may increase overfitting risk. Therefore, the loss plot should be interpreted together with cross-validation performance in Task 3.a rather than choosing the largest network only because it has a low training loss.

Hyperparameter Tuning for Naive Bayes¶

The smoothing parameter alpha was tuned using 5-fold cross-validation.The results show that smaller alpha values achieved better performance, with alpha = 0.01 producing the highest weighted F1-score. A smaller alpha applies weaker Laplace smoothing, allowing the model to preserve stronger differences between informative words. As alpha increases, the probabilities become more smoothed, reducing the impact of highly discriminative words and slightly lowering classification performance.

Task 3.a: kNN 5-fold Cross Validation Parameter Tuning¶

For my kNN part, I focused on tuning the number of neighbours k. I used 5-fold cross-validation to compare different k values and chose the best one based on weighted F1-score.

    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(max_features=1000)),
    ("svd", TruncatedSVD(n_components=100, random_state=42)),

])

}

# use 5-fold cross-validation to compare different k values

)

For my kNN tuning part, I focused on the number of neighbours k. I tested k values of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 15 using 5-fold cross-validation. I used weighted F1-score to compare the results.

Before applying kNN, I used TF-IDF to turn the article text into numerical features. I also used TruncatedSVD to reduce the feature size, because TF-IDF creates many sparse text features and kNN can be affected by high-dimensional data.

The result shows that k changes the performance of the model. A smaller k can make the model more sensitive to nearby training examples, while a larger k usually gives a smoother result. In my result, the best setting was k = 11 with Euclidean distance. The best cross-validation weighted F1-score was about 0.977, and the test weighted F1-score was about 0.9811.

ANN cross-validation discussion¶

For ANN tuning, I compared the number of hidden units and the learning rate using 5-fold cross-validation with weighted F1. The hidden-unit parameter controls model capacity: very small networks may underfit, while larger networks can fit richer patterns but may become less stable. The learning rate controls the size of the weight updates. In these results, the best setting is selected by cross-validation rather than by training loss alone, so the chosen ANN balances fitting ability and generalisation.

Model Comparison Discussion¶

The four classifiers achieved similar performance on the BBC news classification task.

SVM achieved the highest weighted F1 score. This is expected because TF-IDF text features are sparse and often approximately linearly separable.

kNN also performed well, although distance-based methods can become less reliable in high-dimensional feature spaces.

Naive Bayes achieved competitive performance despite its strong independence assumptions.

ANN produced stable results, but its performance was more sensitive to hyperparameter choices such as the number of hidden units.

Task 3(c): Impact of Training Data Size¶

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') # Suppress warnings for small dataset splits

# Assuming X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test are already loaded from Task 1
N = X_train.shape[0]
m_values = [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]

# Inheriting the best hyperparameters from the team's cross-validation (Task 3a & 3b)
best_models = {
    "Naive Bayes": MultinomialNB(alpha=0.01),
    "kNN": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=11, metric='euclidean'),
    "SVM": SVC(kernel='linear', C=1),
    "ANN": MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(40,), learning_rate_init=0.01, max_iter=100, random_state=42)
}

# Initialize dictionaries to store the F1 scores
train_f1_scores = {name: [] for name in best_models}
test_f1_scores = {name: [] for name in best_models}

for m in m_values:
    # Slice the first m portion of the training data
    limit = int(m * N)
    X_train_sub = X_train[:limit]
    y_train_sub = y_train[:limit]

    for name, model in best_models.items():
        # Train on the subset
        model.fit(X_train_sub, y_train_sub)

        # Predict on the subset and the full test set
        y_train_pred = model.predict(X_train_sub)
        y_test_pred = model.predict(X_test)

        # Calculate weighted F1 score using standard sklearn implementation
        train_f1 = f1_score(y_train_sub, y_train_pred, average='weighted')
        test_f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_test_pred, average='weighted')

        train_f1_scores[name].append(train_f1)
        test_f1_scores[name].append(test_f1)

# Plotting the Learning Curves
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))

# Plot (i): Train Accuracy
for name in best_models:
    axes[0].plot(m_values, train_f1_scores[name], marker='o', label=name)
axes[0].set_title('Train Accuracy (F1) vs. Training Size ($m$)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Fraction of Training Data ($m$)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('F1 Score')
axes[0].set_xticks(m_values)
axes[0].grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
axes[0].legend()

# Plot (ii): Test Accuracy
for name in best_models:
    axes[1].plot(m_values, test_f1_scores[name], marker='o', label=name)
axes[1].set_title('Test Accuracy (F1) vs. Training Size ($m$)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Fraction of Training Data ($m$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('F1 Score')
axes[1].set_xticks(m_values)
axes[1].grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

General Trend of Training Accuracy (Train F1 vs. m):

  • Observation: The training accuracy typically starts extremely high (often close to 1.0) when the data fraction is small (m = 0.1) and shows a slight downward trend or stabilization as m increases towards 0.9.
  • Explanation: When the training dataset is very small, the classifiers (especially complex ones like ANN or SVM) can easily memorize the specific vocabulary of those few articles, leading to near-perfect training scores. As the training set grows, the models encounter more variance, noise, and overlapping vocabulary between the "tech" and "entertainment" classes. It becomes harder to perfectly fit all data points, causing the training accuracy to naturally drop slightly and converge to a more realistic baseline.

General Trend of Testing Accuracy (Test F1 vs. m):

  • Observation: The testing accuracy starts at its lowest point at m = 0.1, climbs sharply as more data is introduced, and eventually plateaus or stabilizes as m approaches 0.9.
  • Explanation: At m = 0.1, the models have not seen enough diverse vocabulary to generalize well to unseen data, resulting in poorer performance on the test set. As m increases, the models are exposed to a much richer and more representative distribution of words for both categories. This allows them to learn robust, generalizable decision boundaries rather than memorizing noise. The curve eventually flattens out when the models reach their learning capacity for this specific feature space, meaning additional training data provides diminishing returns.

Task 4: Insights Summary¶

This group project successfully investigated supervised learning algorithms for text classification. Task 1 established the data properties, while Task 2 studied each model family separately. Task 3 brought the models back into the same evaluation framework using 5-fold cross-validation and training-size experiments.

1. Findings from EDA and Feature Extraction The dataset is highly suitable for supervised text classification. The two classes are reasonably balanced. Using CountVectorizer, we extracted 13,518 training features, which is large enough to capture topic-specific vocabulary. The frequency plots demonstrate that the classes are highly separable mainly through vocabulary distribution: Tech articles heavily feature terms like "users", "software", and "microsoft", whereas Entertainment articles are dominated by "film", "music", and "awards".

2. Model-Level Conclusions

  • Naive Bayes is the most interpretable. Its likelihood-ratio words are highly descriptive because they successfully filter out frequent general news terms and highlight the true discriminative words.
  • kNN performs well (Test F1: 0.9811) when using Euclidean distance with $k=11$. Smaller $k$ values make the decision boundary overly sensitive to local noise, while larger $k$ values smooth it out appropriately.
  • SVM provides the strongest and most robust overall result, reaching a Test F1-score of 0.9811 with a Linear kernel ($C=1$). Increasing $C$ makes the soft-margin boundary less tolerant of misclassifications, while the RBF kernel width ($\gamma$) controls the locality of the non-linear boundary.
  • ANN also performs strongly, with the number of hidden units dictating its representational capacity. However, as demonstrated by the loss curves, increasing hidden units must be monitored via validation to prevent overfitting.

3. Hyperparameter and Training-Size Insights Cross-validation confirmed that hyperparameter tuning is critical even on highly separable data. Furthermore, the training-size experiment (Task 3c) revealed an expected pattern:

  • Train Accuracy starts near 1.0 at $m=0.1$ due to early memorization, and slightly stabilizes as data variance increases.
  • Test Accuracy improves significantly as $m$ increases from 0.1 to 0.3, because the models are exposed to a more comprehensive vocabulary distribution, eventually saturating as the models reach their predictive capacity.

Final Recommendation: For maximum predictive reliability, the Linear SVM is the optimal choice for this dataset. However, for reporting and interpretability, Naive Bayes remains highly valuable as its probability ratios directly explain the classification logic.
